subsection: 10. State and culture, North and South: language, religion, education and cultural identity, 1920–1949

notes.h: Two new states, two cultural identities
notes.b: Both parts of Ireland were brand new in the early 1920s, and each government used language, religion, schools and culture to build or defend a sense of who its people were. The South promoted a Gaelic and Catholic identity, the North a Protestant and British one.
points: Northern Ireland was created in 1920-21 under the Government of Ireland Act 1920, and the Free State came into being in December 1922, so both states had to decide what kind of society they wanted.

In the South the cultural programme came from the Gaelic revival before 1914, led by the Gaelic League (which promoted the Irish language) and the GAA (the Gaelic Athletic Association, which promoted Irish games). The Church was the dominant institution, and after 1922 the Protestant minority was small.
In the North the state was run by Unionists, who wanted to keep the link with Britain, and Catholics were about a third of the population, so they were a large minority and not a tiny one.

Conformity means pressure to follow the accepted values, here Catholic and Gaelic ones, enforced through law, schools and public opinion. This is why those who did not fit, such as Protestants or writers, could feel left out.

Censorship is state control of what may be shown or read, carried out by film and publications censors who had the power to ban. Discrimination is unequal treatment of one group; in the North it was aimed at Catholics, including in school funding and control.
notes.tip: A common weakness is writing only about the South. Examiners reward answers that state the identity each state promoted (Gaelic and Catholic; Protestant and British) and explain that each left a minority out.

notes.h: Irish language policy in the Free State
notes.b: The Free State made reviving Irish (which had become a minority language) a central aim of cultural policy. It used schools and the civil service to spread it, and tied knowing Irish to getting a job.
points: Irish became a compulsory subject in national schools (primary schools) in 1922, and infant classes were taught wholly through Irish. This was a change in national schools only; second-level requirements came later.

A pass in Irish became necessary for State examinations at second level and for entry to the civil service and the Garda, so that knowing the language was tied to careers. No exact year is given for these rules, which belong to the 1920s and 1930s.
Ernest Blythe, Minister for Finance from 1923 to 1932, was a leading advocate of Irish, and the civil service was required to learn it.
The Gaeltacht Commission (the Gaeltacht is the Irish-speaking districts) was set up in 1925 and reported in 1926. It defined those districts and recommended economic and educational support for them.
An Gúm was founded in 1926 to publish books in Irish, including translations of foreign works, so that schools had texts and readers in the language.

Taibhdhearc na Gaillimhe, an Irish-language theatre, opened in Galway in 1928. Preparatory colleges trained teachers who could teach through Irish, because the policy depended on teachers able to do so.
The 1937 constitution recognised Irish as the first official language, with English as the second.
notes.tip: For language questions, list the measures with dates (compulsory Irish 1922, the Gaeltacht Commission 1925-26, An Gúm 1926) and then assess the results. Do not say Irish became compulsory in secondary schools in 1922.

notes.b: The policy raised the number of people who could say they knew Irish, but few used it in daily life. Judging it means weighing the census figures against what happened in everyday speech.
points: Census returns showed that about 18 per cent of people said they could speak Irish in 1926, rising to nearly a quarter by 1936. The rise came mainly through schooling, so it measured what pupils had learned and not what they spoke at home.
The Gaeltacht, the real Irish-speaking districts, continued to shrink because of emigration and poverty, so the policy failed to protect the places where Irish was a living language.
Many parents and teachers resented the compulsion, and some pupils learned little, which weakened support for the policy.
Irish remained a symbol of national identity, so the state kept it as a school subject even where it failed as a spoken language.
notes.tip: Say whether the policy succeeded and why it fell short: more knowledge of Irish, little everyday use, a shrinking Gaeltacht. Include the symbolic role of Irish to show balance.

notes.h: Education and the Catholic Church in the South
notes.b: In the Free State the Church ran most schools and the state accepted its role. The state paid for education but left control largely to the clergy.
points: National schools were managed by clergy of the local denomination, and the state paid teachers' salaries and set the curriculum, so the Church controlled the running of schools while the state supplied the money.
The School Attendance Act of 1926 made school attendance compulsory for children from 6 to 14.
Secondary schools were mostly fee-paying and run by religious orders, so few working-class children reached them and access for the poor was limited.
The Vocational Education Act of 1930 set up vocational education committees to provide technical education, a route outside the fee-paying secondary schools.
The Church influenced the content of teaching, and the 1937 constitution recognised the family and the Church's role.
John Charles McQuaid, Archbishop of Dublin from 1940, was an influential voice on social and educational issues.

notes.h: Catholic ethos, censorship and conformity in the South
notes.b: Laws in the Free State reflected Catholic teaching on morality, and critics saw the result as an enforced conformity. Each law below can be dated and linked to that ethos.
points: The Censorship of Films Act of 1923 set up a film censor who could cut or ban films, so what people saw at the cinema was controlled from the start of the state.

In 1925 the Dáil changed its standing orders (its own rules) so that private bills for divorce could no longer be introduced. W.B. Yeats made a famous speech in the Seanad defending the Protestant minority, who did not share the Catholic view of divorce.
The Censorship of Publications Act of 1929 set up a board with the power to ban books and periodicals considered indecent or immoral.
Writers were banned, among them Samuel Beckett (More Pricks Than Kicks, 1934) and, later, Kate O'Brien and Seán Ó Faoláin. A banned writer is good evidence of censorship.
The Public Dance Halls Act of 1935 required dance halls to be licensed, after clerical concern about dances.
The Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1935 banned the sale and import of contraceptives, in line with Catholic teaching.
Article 41 of the 1937 constitution, on the family, banned divorce, and Article 44 recognised the special position of the Catholic Church (it also named other churches and Jewish congregations).

The Protestant population of the Free State fell in the 1920s and 1930s, partly through emigration, the Ne Temere rule (the Church rule on the religion of children of mixed marriages) and the violence of the revolution and Civil War. No figure is given.
notes.tip: Link each law to the Catholic ethos with its date: 1923 films, 1929 publications, 1935 contraceptives and dance halls, divorce 1925 and 1937. Do not mix up the 1925 standing order with the 1937 ban, or Article 41 (the family) with Article 44 (the Church).

notes.h: Cultural institutions and identity in the Free State
notes.b: The state promoted a national culture through games, theatre, radio and the collection of folklore, while the GAA enforced a cultural boundary. Behind all of this lay the ideal of a Gaelic and Catholic Ireland.
points: The Tailteann Games were held in Dublin in 1924, 1928 and 1932, a festival of sport and the arts modelled on the ancient Irish games and open to people of Irish descent abroad.

The Abbey Theatre received a state subsidy from 1925, regarded as the first state subsidy for a national theatre in the English-speaking world. The Gate Theatre was founded in 1928 by Hilton Edwards and Micheál Mac Liammóir to stage international plays.
The state radio station 2RN began broadcasting from Dublin on 1 January 1926, a high-power transmitter at Athlone opened in 1932, and the station was renamed Radio Éireann in 1938.

The Irish Folklore Commission was established in 1935 under Séamus Ó Duilearga to record traditional stories and customs. In the Schools' Collection of 1937-38, primary pupils collected local folklore.
The GAA's Rule 27, in the rulebook from 1905, banned members from playing foreign games such as soccer, rugby, hockey and cricket, and was later extended to attending them. It was repealed in 1971.
In 1938 the GAA removed Douglas Hyde, President of Ireland, as its patron after he attended an international soccer match in Dublin. Hyde had founded the Gaelic League in 1893.

Culture was linked to nationalism by the idea of a Gaelic and Catholic Ireland, which excluded many Protestants and urban people, because it measured Irishness by language, religion and rural tradition.
notes.tip: Do not confuse 2RN (1926) with Radio Éireann (1938), or the Tailteann Games (1924, 1928, 1932) with the Eucharistic Congress. Rule 27 was in force from 1905 to 1971, and was not abolished in 1938.

notes.b: Education was contested between the Unionist government, which wanted a non-denominational state system, and the churches. The outcome was a school system split by religion.
points: The Lynn Committee was appointed in 1921 to review education under the first Minister of Education, Lord Londonderry, and reported in 1922-23.

The Education Act (Northern Ireland) 1923, known as the Londonderry Act, created education committees run by local authorities, with public elementary schools to be non-denominational, that is, free of church control.

Protestant churches and the Orange Order objected to the lack of religious instruction, so the Act was amended in 1925 to allow Bible instruction, and the Orange Order and clergy gained places on school committees.
The Catholic Church refused to transfer its schools to state control and kept them as voluntary schools, outside the state system, with only partial public funding.

The 1930 Amendment Act gave committees of transferred schools four representatives of the transferors (the churches that handed over their schools) and two of the local authority, which Catholics saw as favouring Protestant interests.
The result was a divided school system, which remained a source of segregation and a grievance for Catholics, an example of discrimination.
notes.tip: Remember that the Londonderry Act was named after Lord Londonderry, not Craig, and that the Lynn Committee was the review before it. Give the three dates 1923, 1925 and 1930 to show the dispute developing.

notes.b: In the North the unionist and nationalist communities expressed separate identities in a state that favoured the first. This was the Northern counterpart of the Southern Gaelic and Catholic ideal.
points: Orange Order parades on 12 July and loyalist bands were central to unionist culture and enjoyed official protection.
The Protestant ethos of the state was symbolised by the flag, the Union Jack, and by the royal visits and ceremonies at Stormont.
Nationalists supported the GAA, Irish-language classes and Catholic schools, but the Irish language received little state support.
Under the Special Powers Act (1922) the authorities could ban processions and emblems, and nationalist parades were more likely to be banned, so the law fell unevenly on the two communities.

James Craig (Lord Craigavon), the prime minister, said in 1934 that it was "a Protestant Parliament and a Protestant State". This was matched in the South by the Catholic emphasis of the 1937 constitution.
notes.tip: Examiners reward the Northern education dispute and loyalist culture as the paired half of an answer on North and South. Use only Craig's short phrase, attributed to him.

notes.b: Hone was a leading modernist painter who turned to stained glass and became the best-known Irish stained-glass artist of her time. Her career shows how art could express an independent Ireland's identity.
points: Evie Hone (1894-1955) was born in Dublin and studied art in London and later in Paris under André Lhote and Albert Gleizes.
With Mainie Jellett she was one of the first Irish painters to work in a cubist style, which breaks a subject into geometric shapes.
From the 1930s she worked in stained glass with An Túr Gloine (the Tower of Glass), the Dublin studio founded by Sarah Purser in 1903 to revive Irish stained glass.
She converted to Catholicism in 1937, and much of her work was for churches, so church patronage shaped her career.
My Four Green Fields, a window symbolising the four provinces, was made for the Irish pavilion at the 1939 New York World's Fair.
The Crucifixion east window of Eton College Chapel was commissioned in 1949 to replace glass destroyed by a bomb in 1940, and was installed in 1952.
Contemporaries praised her work as modern Irish art of international standing.
Later writers on Irish art place her in the effort to give independent Ireland a modern cultural identity.
notes.tip: For a paragraph on Hone, give birth and education (Dublin 1894; London and Paris; Lhote and Gleizes), cubism with Jellett, stained glass from the 1930s with An Túr Gloine, and a named work with its date. Do not confuse her with Mainie Jellett, who was a cubist painter and not a stained-glass artist.

notes.h: Assessment: cultural policy, achievements and limits
notes.b: Cultural policy gave each state a distinct identity, but it also narrowed the range of what was acceptable. Each state promoted the identity of its own majority community.
points: Achievement: institutions such as An Gúm, the Folklore Commission, the Abbey and Radio Éireann preserved and promoted Irish culture, giving the new state a distinct identity.
Limit: compulsory Irish did not make it the daily language of most people, and the Gaeltacht continued to decline.
Achievement: arts and crafts, including the work of Hone, flourished with state and church patronage.
Limit: censorship and moral legislation restricted writers and individual choice, and minorities felt excluded, which produced conformity.
In the North the divided education system and separate cultural traditions deepened the communal division, in contrast with the South, where the state and the majority shared one cultural ideal.
Contemporary view: supporters saw cultural policy as defending Irish identity; critics, including writers such as Ó Faoláin, saw a narrow and conformist vision.
Later view: historians stress the tension between revival and restriction, and the influence of the Church.
notes.tip: A strong essay states its judgement at the start, balances North and South, and supports it with dated facts: Irish in schools, the Gaeltacht Commission, the censorship acts, the 1937 constitution, and the Londonderry Act with its amendments.

In the North, the unequal treatment of Catholics, including in schools, where Catholic schools were funded less than state schools.
The 1925–26 body that defined Irish-speaking districts and recommended support for them.
The state publishing agency for Irish-language books, founded in 1926.
The body set up in 1935 to collect and archive oral tradition.
